strengths: Timely and relevant problem: evaluating ML engineering agents in community-driven settings is important, and the paper clearly motivates why isolated-agent benchmarks miss a key part of real Kaggle-style workflows.
MLE-Live is a potentially useful benchmark direction, incorporating public discussions, kernels, metadata, leaderboards, and both offline and live competition evaluation.
The empirical results are promising: CoMind improves average win rate over AIDE variants on 20 competitions and is additionally tested through real submissions to four ongoing Kaggle competitions.
The comparison uses a strong prior agent baseline with the same backend LLM, and the paper includes reasonable variants such as AIDE+Code and AIDE+RAG to probe the role of community knowledge.
The agent design is intuitive and practically motivated, with idea pools, report pools, iterative implementation, and shared reports across agents reflecting aspects of human collaborative ML work.
weaknesses: The methodological details are insufficient for a top-tier paper: prompts, retrieval/summarization procedures, idea/report pool construction, multi-agent scheduling, and exact competition/task list are not described in enough detail to make the work reproducible.

The evaluation raises fairness and compute-budget questions. CoMind appears to benefit from richer access to many public artifacts and possibly parallel/shared-agent operation, while AIDE+Code and AIDE+RAG are simplified augmentations; it is unclear whether all systems receive comparable context, retrieval quality, and compute.

The benchmark may be vulnerable to leakage or memorization through public Kaggle kernels and discussions. Although artifacts are said to be pre-deadline, the paper does not rigorously analyze whether agents can effectively copy high-performing public solutions, nor how this affects claims of novel ML engineering ability.

Ablations are very limited. The main ablation only removes public resources; it does not isolate idea selection, idea generation, report pools, multi-agent sharing, parallel drafts, retrieval strategy, or the effect of public kernels versus discussions.

Statistical reliability is weak: results seem to be single runs over 20 tasks, with no confidence intervals, variance across seeds/runs, significance tests, or robustness analysis despite stochastic LLM behavior.

The novelty evaluation is under-specified. The paper does not report the number of expert raters, blinding, rubric, inter-rater agreement, examples of novel ideas, or how copied/modified public-code ideas were excluded.
Some claimed evidence is not convincing: code length is treated as a proxy for sophistication, but longer code may also reflect verbosity, inefficiency, or overfitting rather than better reasoning.

The ethical and community impact discussion is shallow for a system that submits to live Kaggle competitions and may affect human participants; competition policy compliance, disclosure, and risks of benchmark contamination deserve more serious treatment.

The technical contribution of CoMind is mostly a system composition of known ideas such as retrieval, iterative coding agents, memory pools, and multi-agent sharing, with limited algorithmic novelty beyond the application setting.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating ML-engineering agents in settings that include community knowledge rather than isolated benchmark tasks.
The proposed MLE-Live setup is conceptually appealing, and the paper makes a reasonable case that Kaggle discussions and public kernels are relevant resources for realistic agent evaluation.
The experiments compare against AIDE and two community-augmented variants, and include both past competitions and a small set of live Kaggle submissions.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is not convincing. Giving agents access to public kernels, public scores, author tiers, and end-to-end community solutions risks measuring retrieval, copying, and leaderboard-aware reuse rather than autonomous ML-engineering capability. The paper does not sufficiently control for leakage or distinguish genuine innovation from recombination of existing public solutions.

The baseline comparison appears unfair or under-specified. CoMind has a rich idea/report-pool mechanism over community artifacts, while AIDE+Code receives only one top-voted kernel per node and AIDE+RAG uses a relatively simple retrieval procedure. It is unclear whether the gains come from the proposed agent design or from stronger access/selection over public resources.

Reproducibility is weak. The paper lacks detailed prompts, exact competition list and splits, artifact filtering procedure, implementation details for the community simulation, number of agents/iterations, run-to-run variance, costs, and whether code/data will be released.

The ablation study is far too limited. It only removes public resources, but does not isolate the contributions of idea selection, idea generation, report pool, multi-agent sharing, parallel drafts, metadata such as votes/public scores, or retrieval/summarization choices.

The statistical evidence is thin. Results are averaged over only 20 competitions with some categories containing one task, no confidence intervals or repeated runs are reported, and claims of state-of-the-art performance are stronger than the evidence supports.

Several evaluation proxies are questionable. Code length is treated as evidence of sophistication, but longer code is not necessarily better. The novelty evaluation is described only briefly, with no expert protocol, annotation criteria, inter-rater agreement, or examples of allegedly novel ideas.

The live Kaggle evaluation is too small and potentially ethically/methodologically problematic. Submitting automated agents to ongoing competitions raises concerns about compliance, leaderboard probing, and effects on human participants, but the discussion is minimal.

The writing often overclaims. Statements about democratizing ML, contributing meaningfully to scientific research, and achieving novel solutions are not adequately supported by the experiments presented.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: current ML-engineering agents are usually evaluated in isolated settings, while real Kaggle-style work relies heavily on public discussions, kernels, and iterative community knowledge. The MLE-Live framing is compelling and relevant.

CoMind is a plausible and well-motivated agent design. The idea/report pools, staged idea selection and generation, constrained implementation loop, and multi-agent shared-report mechanism are a coherent response to the community-driven setting rather than a superficial RAG add-on.

The empirical results are encouraging. On 20 Kaggle competitions, CoMind improves over AIDE and community-augmented AIDE variants in aggregate win rate, above-median rate, valid submissions, and medals, and the live submissions on four ongoing Kaggle competitions add useful external validity.

The baselines include a strong prior system, AIDE, plus two extensions intended to give AIDE access to community resources. This makes the central comparison more meaningful than only comparing against closed-world agents.
The paper includes useful ablations showing that public resources improve CoMind, as well as an attempt to evaluate novelty rather than only leaderboard performance.
weaknesses: Several key implementation and evaluation details are underspecified, limiting reproducibility: prompts, retrieval/summarization procedures, exact idea/report pool construction, number of parallel agents, iteration schedules, compute/cost, and release plans for MLE-Live are not described in enough detail.

The community-resource setting raises leakage and fairness concerns that need a more rigorous treatment. Public kernels may contain near-complete solutions, and the paper does not sufficiently analyze how much of CoMind's gain comes from copying/adapting strong public notebooks versus genuinely synthesizing new approaches.

The comparison to human competitors is somewhat overstated. Kaggle leaderboard win rate is an imperfect measure because competitors vary widely in effort, submissions may be stale, and agents are evaluated with fixed hardware/time and access to curated community artifacts. Claims such as “outperforms 79.2% human competitors” should be framed more cautiously.

The baseline adaptations may not be strong enough. AIDE+Code uses only one top-voted kernel per node, while AIDE+RAG appears relatively simple; stronger retrieval, notebook-selection, ensemble, or AutoML-style baselines could narrow the gap.

The evaluation lacks variance estimates, repeated runs, statistical tests, and per-task detailed results. Since LLM-agent performance can be highly stochastic, aggregate averages over 20 tasks without uncertainty make it hard to judge robustness.

Some metrics and analyses are weak proxies. Code length is treated as evidence of sophistication, but longer code is not necessarily better. The novelty evaluation is promising but underdescribed: expert identities, rubric, inter-rater agreement, blinding, and examples of novel ideas are missing.

The live evaluation is valuable but small, with only four ongoing competitions, and includes cases with small participant pools. This supports practicality but is not enough for the strongest claims about general real-world deployment.

The paper needs clearer positioning of the benchmark contribution relative to MLE-Bench and DSBench, especially what is newly curated, how test labels/graders are built, and whether the benchmark can be safely released without violating Kaggle terms or competition norms.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: evaluating ML-engineering agents in settings where community artifacts, public code, and discussions influence performance, rather than only isolated closed-world benchmarks.
MLE-Live is a potentially useful evaluation direction, with temporal filtering of public Kaggle artifacts and a sizable collection of discussions/kernels across 75 competitions.
CoMind is a coherent multi-agent system with sensible roles for analysis, ideation, coding, evaluation, and iterative refinement, and the paper provides substantial prompt detail in the appendix.
The reported empirical results are strong on their face: 36% Any Medal on 75 MLE-Bench competitions and competitive ranks on eight ongoing Kaggle competitions.
The ablations against AIDE variants with code/RAG access are useful and support the claim that structured use of community resources can outperform simpler retrieval or code-injection baselines.
weaknesses: The main benchmark comparison is not fully apples-to-apples: CoMind has access to public Kaggle kernels/discussions, while many leaderboard baselines were designed/evaluated in more isolated MLE-Bench settings. This makes the claimed state of the art hard to interpret as agentic capability rather than effective reuse/adaptation of public solutions.

The paper does not sufficiently address leakage and contamination risks from public Kaggle artifacts. Even if artifacts are timestamped before deadlines and public datasets are restricted, kernels may encode leaderboard-driven decisions, pseudo-labeling strategies, external resources, or near-complete solutions, which can substantially change the benchmark semantics.

The live Kaggle evaluation is interesting but limited: only eight competitions, no controlled concurrent baselines, unclear variance across runs, and no detailed accounting of submissions, leaderboard probing, or how public/private leaderboard differences affect the reported ranks.

The ablation study is too narrow to isolate the contribution of each CoMind component. It compares against AIDE variants and CoMind without resources, but does not cleanly ablate Coordinator/Analyzer/Idea Proposer/Evaluator, number of parallel agents, compute budget, memory, or resource selection strategy.

Compute and budget fairness are under-specified. CoMind uses multiple parallel coding agents and 24-hour runs in the main evaluation, while comparisons rely partly on external leaderboard numbers or different scaffolds; normalized compute/cost comparisons are missing.

Reproducibility remains uncertain. The paper includes prompts and aggregate statistics, but the exact benchmark construction, scraping/filtering rules, dependency handling, selected artifacts, run seeds, generated submissions, and code release status are not sufficiently specified for independent verification.

The ethical and practical implications of deploying autonomous agents in ongoing Kaggle competitions are under-discussed, including competition rules, effects on human leaderboards, use of public community work, and disclosure/consent considerations.

Some analysis is weakly justified: code length/complexity is treated as evidence of richer solutions, but longer code is not necessarily better; stronger qualitative and causal analysis of successful/failed strategies would improve the paper.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating and building ML engineering agents that can use public community knowledge, rather than operating in an isolated benchmark setting.

MLE-Live is a potentially useful evaluation direction. The attempt to preserve timestamps for Kaggle discussions/kernels and to include live ongoing competitions addresses a real weakness of static agent benchmarks.

The paper reports results on a relatively broad set of Kaggle-style tasks, including 75 retrospective MLE-Bench competitions, a 20-task ablation subset, and eight ongoing competitions. This breadth is a positive aspect of the submission.

The multi-agent system is intuitively organized into coordinator, analyzer, idea proposer, coding agent, and evaluator roles, and the appendix provides some qualitative prompts/case-study material that helps clarify intended operation.
weaknesses: The central empirical comparison is not fair or convincing. CoMind is compared against MLE-Bench leaderboard agents while being given access to public Kaggle kernels and discussions, whereas many baselines were evaluated in isolated settings without the same community information. This makes the claimed state-of-the-art result difficult to interpret.

The paper has serious contamination and leakage concerns. Public Kaggle kernels and discussions often encode extensive human engineering, leaderboard feedback, task-specific tricks, and sometimes leakage-based heuristics. Even with timestamp filtering and external dataset restrictions, using these artifacts can make the benchmark measure reuse of public human solutions more than autonomous ML engineering ability.

The novelty of CoMind itself is limited. The architecture is a fairly standard role-specialized multi-agent coding system with retrieval/use of public artifacts, parallel coding agents, and local validation. The paper does not provide a technically deep new algorithm or a rigorous analysis of why this design is better than simpler retrieval-plus-agent baselines.

The ablation study is insufficient. It uses only 20 competitions, does not isolate individual components of CoMind clearly enough, and the strongest comparisons are variants of AIDE with relatively simple resource access. There is no careful compute-matched comparison against stronger agent scaffolds with the same public kernels, same number of parallel workers, same LLM, and same time budget.

The live Kaggle results are suggestive but not a reliable scientific evaluation. They are based on only eight competitions, public leaderboard rank may not reflect final/private leaderboard performance, and the protocol is underspecified regarding submission limits, timing, retries, manual intervention, and whether the agent's participation could affect the competition ecosystem.

The benchmark construction is underdescribed relative to its importance. The manuscript does not give enough detail on scraping, filtering, deduplication, dependency reconstruction, handling deleted/edited kernels, private/public leaderboard alignment, reconstructed test sets, or how exact reproducibility of MLE-Live would be ensured.

The methodology section is often high-level and imprecise. Key mechanisms such as sampling kernels/discussions, scoring artifacts, selecting ideas, publishing new artifacts to the simulated community, and aggregating parallel agent results are described narratively rather than as a precise algorithm with enough implementation detail.

Several claims are overstated. The paper frames CoMind as simulating community-driven research and producing novel solutions, but much of the performance may come from adapting high-vote public notebooks. The paper does not adequately separate original agent innovation from recombination of existing human work.

The evaluation metrics are narrow. Any Medal, win rate, and above-median performance are useful but insufficient; the paper should also report robustness across random seeds, variance across runs, cost-normalized performance, private leaderboard stability, failure rates, and the marginal value of each source of community information.

Reproducibility remains weak despite extensive appendices. The paper reports prompts and token costs, but does not clearly commit to releasing the benchmark, scraped artifacts, dependency graphs, execution environment, agent code, run logs, and exact outputs needed to audit such a complex system.

strengths: Timely and relevant problem: evaluating ML engineering agents in community-driven settings is important, and MLE-Live addresses a real limitation of isolated Kaggle-style benchmarks.

Strong empirical headline results: CoMind reports state-of-the-art medal rate on 75 MLE-Bench competitions and credible live performance across eight ongoing Kaggle competitions, which is more convincing than purely retrospective evaluation.

The paper includes useful controlled ablations on 20 tasks with the same backend model, showing that CoMind outperforms AIDE variants and that access to community resources materially improves performance.

The system design is coherent: separating analysis, idea proposal, coding, evaluation, and coordination matches the structure of ML experimentation and is supported by detailed prompts and a case study.
Appendices provide substantial implementation context, including prompts, token costs, dataset statistics, and a detailed denoising case study, which helps interpret how the agent works in practice.
weaknesses: The central comparison in Table 1 is not fully controlled: baseline numbers are taken from an external leaderboard and use different models, scaffolds, compute budgets, and possibly different resource access assumptions. This weakens the claim of state-of-the-art superiority.

The contribution of the agent versus the contribution of reusing public Kaggle kernels is not cleanly disentangled. Since CoMind can inspect and adapt public code, its performance may partly reflect efficient kernel adaptation rather than novel ML engineering capability.

The paper’s treatment of data leakage and fairness is incomplete. Although artifacts are filtered by competition deadline and public datasets are restricted in some settings, public kernels may encode leaderboard-specific choices, hidden external resources, or competition-specific leakage patterns.

Live Kaggle evaluation is compelling but under-specified ethically and methodologically: the paper does not clearly discuss competition rules, disclosure, effects on human participants, public vs private leaderboard stability, or whether rankings are final.

The method novelty is moderate. The multi-agent decomposition, RAG-like use of public artifacts, iterative coding/debugging, and held-out validation evaluator are sensible but mostly combinations of existing agent-system ideas.

Ablations are useful but still limited: they cover only 20 Lite tasks under a reduced 5-hour setting, and there is no fine-grained ablation of agent roles, number of parallel coders, memory, analyzer scoring, or resource-selection strategy.
Some analytical metrics are weak proxies for quality. For example, longer code and higher complexity are presented positively, but they may also indicate brittleness or overengineering.

Reproducibility remains limited because the system depends on proprietary o4-mini, live Kaggle access, substantial compute, and scraped community artifacts; no clear release plan for code, benchmark artifacts, or exact run logs is stated.
Writing and presentation contain several grammatical errors and occasional unclear phrasing, which does not block understanding but reduces polish for a top-tier submission.
